World.title: Trump pauses 50% tariffs on Canadian goods for 3 days
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced late Tuesday he will pause the implementation of 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods for three days, posting the decision less than two hours before the crushing levies were set to take effect.

In an initial online post, the president said he delayed the levies "based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL!"

A White House declaration later said the suspension is "in the public interest" because Canadian negotiators "expressed a commitment" to concede on trade grievances the Trump administration had cited as the reason for threatening the tariffs in the first place.

In his own statement an hour later, Prime Minister Mark Carney did not speak of a tentative deal and did not say which concessions might have been made. He characterized the administration's decision as a postponement so trade discussions can continue.

"Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done," read the statement.

"While we continue this work, Canada remains focused on building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive economy at home."

WATCH | Tariffs to be delayed for at least 3 days: Trump pauses 50% tariffs, saying new trade deal reached | Duration 6:27 U.S. President Donald Trump has paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, saying the two countries have reached a new trade deal that just needs to be finalized. In a statement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'substantial progress has been made.'

The Trump administration's latest round of tariffs were originally scheduled to take effect at 12:01 a.m. ET on Wednesday. The levies would have applied to hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion, from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks.

The delay buys time for negotiators who had been racing to reach an agreement ahead of the deadline. It also brings some degree of momentary relief to companies on both sides of the border who worried the fees would devastate small businesses, disrupt supply chains and drive up the cost of living for everyday families.

There is no guarantee Canada can dodge tariffs long-term. Trump did not say whether any deal, if finalized, would lead to the levies' permanent cancellation.

Canadian trade representatives have met with their American counterparts in D.C. a number of times in recent weeks for negotiations Carney previously described as "intense" and "delicate." The prime minister spoke to Trump by phone on Monday and earlier Tuesday.

After the Carney-Trump call, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc again spoke to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to try and close the gap in the negotiating positions.

In a statement after Trump's announcement, Greer said the deal included "comprehensive market access for all American goods, economic security commitments, digital trade alignment, and many important provisions that will continue to protect our market and American workers, along with our Canadian partners," without offering specifics.

Trump suggested a deal could revive Keystone XL, a pipeline project that would have moved oil from Alberta to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries. His online post on Tuesday said the venture, cancelled by the Biden administration in 2021, "may be awoken from the grave!"

Auto tariffs have been a sticking point: sources

Earlier Tuesday, sources cautioned that Canada and the U.S. remained at loggerheads over some finer points, including what sort of tariff, if any, will be applied on Canadian autos bound for the U.S.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the talks.

Trump threatened to hit Canada with the 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian products ostensibly in retaliation for Ottawa imposing tariffs on some U.S. goods, tariffs that were only levied after Trump launched his trade war on Canada last year.

WATCH | Trade talks expected up until deadline, adviser says: Trade talks with U.S. 'may go down to the wire': Charest | Duration 9:56 With 50 per cent tariffs set to take effect just after midnight, negotiators from Canada and the United States continue to work toward a deal. Member of the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S Economic Relations Jean Charest joins Power & Politics to break down what the state of negotiations means for Canada.

A senior government official previously said Canada was working on a response in the event those tariffs came into effect.

Carney has been weighing a range of options to hit back at the U.S. on trade, including more retaliatory tariffs, the official said. Canada had planned to see the legally binding paperwork on these prospective U.S. tariffs before deciding on an appropriate response.

A key issue in the negotiations has been just how much Canada can get out of the U.S. in exchange for a series of concessions of its own.

LeBlanc has pushed for the U.S. to scrap the new Section 338 tariffs but also lower the existing Section 232 tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

WATCH | Entrepreneur says tariffs would ruin his livelihood: Michigan furniture maker says U.S. tariffs threaten his family business | Duration 6:52 Michael Howard, owner of Howard Family Designs, a custom furniture business in Warren, Mich., and says the Trump administration's tariffs on lumber and other goods are driving up costs, making them lose orders and putting his shop's community mentorship program on hold.

The Americans want U.S. liquor back on the shelves of provincially run stores, ending a boycott that has been devastatingly effective. The Trump administration is also pushing for Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos removed, and tweaks to how the supply-managed dairy sector allocates quotas.

Greer has repeatedly signalled the U.S. is not open to dropping its tariff regime entirely, but there are some signs that the rate may be flexible if the Canadians address some U.S. demands.

Canada wants the U.S. to drive down tariff rates to the lowest possible level, and what's been presented so far by Greer and his team is not satisfactory, sources said.

On autos, the latest U.S. offer would lower the tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles to a headline rate of 15 per cent, down from the current 25 per cent. The headline rate would be the official rate enacted by executive order.

WATCH | NDP on the state of tariff talks: Carney has given 'concession after concession' on U.S. trade: NDP | Duration 0:46 New Democratic Party parliamentary leader Don Davies says Canadians are 'very worried' about the impact new U.S. tariffs could have on Canadian jobs. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian products if a deal isn't reached.

But the tariff on Canadian-made vehicles can be reduced further by having more U.S. content, down to an effective rate (the actual duty rate collected) of 7.5 per cent.

Sources said that is still higher than Canada wants.

The new deadline expires at the end of the day on Friday. In the meantime, some Canadian businesses will keep rushing sales out the door to try and beat any levies. Others have already lost American customers because the situation is too volatile.

Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the United Nations, said Trump's tariffs don't need to take effect to achieve the administration's desired result. The will-they-or-won't-they waiting period creates uncertainty that destabilizes the Canadian economy.

"The whole thing is designed to make Canada feel like a less secure place to do business," Rae told CBC News. "We have to respond in such a way to indicate that, 'No, We're going to continue to go ahead. We're not going to be put off by this.'""

World.title: Why elaborate (and expensive) dorm room decor reveals have taken over TikTok
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There was a time, back in the olden days us elder millennials called "the early 2000s," when dorm room decor consisted of a "bed in a bag," a milk crate and a shower caddy.

It didn't do much to cheer up the cement room you shared with the Bio major you'd never met until orientation day, but it was something — and it was yours.

Now it would seem, at least according to social media, that the prison cell esthetic is no longer a rite of passage.

"Emily and Hadley, are you ready for your grand reveal?" a professional designer said in a TikTok "dorm reveal" video last week before showing two freshmen their new space — complete with ruffled bedspreads, matching canopied headboards, an accent rug, a sectional sofa, soft lighting, framed art and a vanity.

By Tuesday, it had been viewed 1.5 million times.

Dorm room upgrades — and their reveals — are so popular online that there's a #DormTok hashtag where videos can get millions of views, and Facebook groups like " Dorm Rooms of Mississippi and Beyond" where some 80,000 members swap design ideas.

There are countless magazine articles that list dorm room "essentials" such as dust ruffles and monogrammed pillows, and Pinterest boards full of "cottagecore nature dorm room" and "coastal dream dorm room" inspiration. Even Ikea has a dorm room transformation page on its website, with design suggestions for a "modern whimsy" look that comes with about a $2,700 Cdn price tag.

There are interior designers who specialize in dorm rooms and charge as much as $20,000 US. And, most critically: there are parents willing to foot the bill.

A screen grab of a post on Threads from Aug. 15, 2026, by Bobbie Hall Young. (@bobbie_not_old/Threads)

The U.S. National Retail Federation estimates that college back-to-school shoppers will spend about $14 billion US on dorm and apartment furnishings this season — a 10 per cent jump from last year.

In another video posted this week, a professional designer shows off "all the details" for a dorm room makeover at the University of Mississippi, including floor-length drapes, a carpet runner, a ruffled white couch with throw pillows, side tables, lamps, a coffee table, custom-built padded desk chairs, custom-built headboards, bedside cubbies and matching ottomans to help the girls step into their raised beds.

"Moved the baby of the brood into her dorm at East Tennessee State," posted a mom on Threads earlier this week alongside photos of a similar room makeover: raised beds, matching ottomans, headboards, floral carpeting, and a lit-up makeup vanity on what used to be a desk.

"12 hours to set up but it was worth it," another TikToker writes alongside a video with 3.5 million views where she reveals a carpet, velvet headboard, shelving and floral decor.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by designer Shelly Gates of @MaryMargaretDesigns posted on June 5, 2026. (@MaryMargaretDesigns/Instagram)

What's driving the decor trend?

If you're wondering what-in-the-upholstered-headboard is happening on college campuses these days, you're not alone. The comment sections on the many (and there are many) videos and posts of so-called dorm room reveals flooding social media this month are a mix of admiration, confusion and disbelief.

"Does anyone else think this is insane?" reads a comment on one of the TikTok videos. The comment was liked 30,000 times.

"L iving in a shitty dorm is a part of the college experience," someone commented on another video.

" Remember when we were dropped off wit h a 'bed in a bag' a nd a dream? Take us back," commented another person.

As House Beautiful magazine recently reported, "on-campus living is becoming a full-on design flex," due in part to our influencer culture where curating a certain esthetic has seeped into daily living. And in the U.S. at least, move-in day has become a social media event, reports Today.

The more elaborate dorm transformations being seen online appear to be largely a U.S. trend, and social media is definitely driving their popularity, Trevor Kruse, the CEO of Interior Designers of Canada, told CBC News.

It also doesn't surprise him that student dorm decor is taking off, he added.

"A dorm room is often their first opportunity to create a space of their own that reflects their personalities," Kruse said. "Even small changes to an interior environment can influence mood, productivity, and overall comfort, helping students create a space that supports both learning and downtime."

Mississippi interior designer Shelly Gates, who reportedly charges as much as $20,000 US for a dorm room makeover, says the goal is to make the spaces feel "warm, happy and like home."

"Most dorms start out with cinderblock walls and fluorescent lighting, and honestly, they can feel a little cold and intimidating," Gates told the New York Post last week.

WATCH | People keep hurting themselves in these Zara pants: Why these trendy Zara pants are called 'death trousers’ | Duration 1:20 I'm sure many of us enjoy a stylish pair of pants — but not if they cause injuries. That's apparently what's happening to people wearing one of Zara's trending trousers. CBC's Puneet Nijjar explains what the heck is going on.

Is it happening here?

Decorating your own space isn't new. But while professional-grade overhauls appear to be mostly in the U.S. — and especially the southern states — there are signs a more subdued version of the trend could be creeping north.

On Pinterest Canada, for instance, dorm-related searches are trending, while "dorm room" searches on Google Trends are up 40 per cent compared to this time last year. On Facebook, there's a "University Dorm Room Moms - Canada" group with 13,000 members posting practical questions about under-bed storage space, mattress toppers and duvets.

And Canadian retailer Simons has a dorm decor section on its website, advertising "w himsical objects, bold patterns and contrasting colours to create a room" with personality.

Kruse notes that while Canadian students certainly personalize their dorm rooms, Canadian schools may have restrictions about how much can be changed.

Audrey Leveridge, 17, says she found some inspiration on Pinterest for her upcoming move into residence at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., and bought some decor based on her preferred colour palette.

"I think lots of people are planning on doing dorm decorations with themes, though," she told CBC News.

"I haven't heard of any overhauls but I know people like to make it look as nice as possible, more homey and their own."

World.title: Israel opens criminal probes over killings of 6-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, Gaza rescue workers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israel's military said on Wednesday that it will open internal investigations over its troops' killings in Gaza of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in January 2024 and 15 emergency and aid workers in March 2025, although rights groups said such probes rarely lead to convictions.

The military said the investigation decisions followed probes by its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism. It released decisions regarding five incidents involving the deaths of Palestinians.

They included an examination of the killings of seven aid workers with the World Central Kitchen charity in April 2024. On that incident, the military said there was "no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation."

"For more than a thousand days, the IDF [Israel Defence Forces] has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality," the Israeli military said.

"As part of the IDF’s obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, the IDF examines exceptional incidents that occurred during combat," the military said.

Both the killing of Rajab in February 2024 and the killing of 15 Palestinian medics in May 2025 gained international attention.

But Israeli rights groups say that criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.

"Nearly zero indictments are served relative to the number of complaints of soldiers and commanders who commit offences. In rare cases when commanders or soldiers are convicted, they receive ridiculously lenient sentences compared with the severity of the offence," said a spokesperson for the Israeli rights organization Yesh Din.

Rajab's grandmother, also named Hind Rajab, told The Associated Press by phone that the Israeli investigation is not enough, and called for an international probe into the killing of her granddaughter and all of the hundreds of children killed in Gaza during the war.

"An international investigation is required to uncover the truth and hold all those responsible accountable," she said. "We call for justice, not only for Hind but for all Gaza children."

In June, a United Nations Human Rights Council report said evidence showed that Israeli security forces had "deliberately targeted" and killed Palestinian children in Gaza. Israel rejected the report as "a propaganda piece."

Phone call begging for help

During Israel's offensive in response to the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, Hind Rajab was pinned down in a car for hours, begging Palestinian medics by mobile phone to send help, while her aunt, uncle and three cousins already lay dead.

When an ambulance arrived, contact with the girl and the rescuers themselves was lost. Twelve days later, the bodies of the girl, her relatives and two ambulance workers were recovered from the area.

A film about Hind Rajab's death, which sparked international outcry, won the Silver Lion Award at the Venice Film Festival and was nominated for an Academy Award.

A destroyed car where the body of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, 6, who begged Gaza rescuers to send help after being trapped by Israeli military fire, was found in Gaza City on Feb. 10, 2024. (Reuters)

In March 2025, 15 emergency and aid workers from the Red Crescent, Palestinian Civil Defense and the United Nations were recovered from a grave in the sand in the south of the Gaza Strip, United Nations officials said at the time.

UN aid chief Tom Fletcher said in a post on X that the bodies were buried near "wrecked & well-marked vehicles," adding: "They were killed by Israeli forces while trying to save lives. We demand answers & justice."

Israeli forces say they have never deliberately targeted civilians in the Gaza war. They say Hamas endangers such people's lives by using them for cover.

The Israeli military did not immediately comment directly on the deaths of the Red Crescent workers at the time. In a later statement to Reuters, it said that it had facilitated the evacuation of the bodies from the area, which it described as an active combat zone. It did not specifically respond to questions about why the bodies were retrieved from beneath the sand or why the vehicles were found crushed.

"More important than opening the investigation is that this should have been prevented," Eid Aziz, media director for the Red Crescent, told Reuters.

"The Palestinian Red Crescent badge is protected by international laws, and the medical staff must be protected, especially as they execute their duties and humanitarian work.”

World.title: Run Terry Run, the upcoming Terry Fox documentary, has a new trailer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The trailer for a new documentary about Terry Fox featuring "never-before-seen" footage was released today, one month ahead of its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).

Using nearly 100 reels of recently recovered archival footage, Run Terry Run promises an inside look at the British Columbia athlete and cancer research advocate's 1980 Marathon of Hope.

The trailer features dialogue and commentary from van driver and friend Doug Alward, Terry Fox's younger brother Darrell Fox, and Terry Fox himself as the 21-year-old attempted to run across Canada to raise money for cancer research after his leg was amputated due to osteogenic sarcoma.

"I think of home a lot. I think of running into Vancouver … where I'm going to finish on the ocean," Fox is heard saying in the trailer.

"To me, I'm happy doing what I'm doing — I wouldn't want to be doing anything else. And so I'm going to keep on going."

WATCH | Run Terry Run trailer:

Toronto director Sean Menard recovered the raw footage from filmmaker John Simpson, who filmed Fox's run with multiple camera operators starting on the East Coast.

Simpson made his own 1981 CBC-sponsored documentary, Terry Fox: I Had A Dream, but he believed the remaining footage had been thrown away, according to an interview Menard did with the Globe and Mail .

Menard, who previously made the self-funded MuchMusic documentary 299 Queen Street West, was inspired to search for first-hand documentation of Fox's marathon due to the limited amount of high-quality footage available. Aided by the Terry Fox Foundation, he discovered the footage in a Toronto storage unit a few blocks from his own home.

He subsequently restored the reels of film to 4K quality and used it to make his film, which he first screened at Toronto's Roy Thomson Hall last year.

According to a Canadian Running review of that screening, the documentary features no "talking head" interviews, instead using voiceovers from Alward, Darrell Fox and two others: Leslie Scrivener, the first journalist to cover the Marathon of Hope; and Darryl Sittler, the then-captain of the Toronto Maple Leafs who ran alongside Terry from Scarborough to Nathan Phillips Square.

Lasting impact

Fox began his marathon April 12, 1980, roughly three years after learning of his cancer diagnosis. His original goal was to run from St. John's to Victoria. He made it 5,373 kilometres before being forced to cut his attempt short near Thunder Bay, Ont., after the cancer spread to his lungs.

Though Fox died in 1981, his marathon raised more than $24 million at the time — $1 for every Canadian. Earlier this year, the Terry Fox Foundation announced it had surpassed $1 billion in funds raised for cancer research.

Fox has been the subject of numerous documentaries before — from Simpson's film, to 1983's The Terry Fox Story, to Into the Wind, an episode of ESPN's 30 For 30 series released in 2010.

In 2024, the Bank of Canada announced Fox's image would appear on the country's next $5 bank note.

In 2025, Menard told The Canadian Press that his film captures "the evolution of a 21-year-old," starting when Fox was a less-confident runner simply propelled by a grand idea.

It eventually finds him as a young man learning to manage the international spotlight while pushing his limits.

An original score for the documentary was recorded by U.S. composer Tom Caffey, who previously worked on the Michael Jordan Netflix docuseries The Last Dance.

Run Terry Run will premiere at TIFF on Sept. 19, one day before the 46th annual Terry Fox Run. It is scheduled for a theatrical release on Oct. 9, 2026.

World.title: Edmonton Marathon apologizes, says detour error lengthened 2026 race distances
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two days after runners completed the Edmonton Marathon, the race director is apologizing after he says event officials discovered an error in accounting for detours that led to race courses being too long.

The acknowledgment confirmed what many runners said they had suspected.

In a statement issued Tuesday afternoon, Edmonton Marathon race director Tom Keogh said the distance of the half-marathon and marathon courses measured 674.7 metres longer than previously thought.

“The Edmonton Marathon’s previous statement detailing confidence in the course certification process was issued with the best information it had at the time,” Keogh said, adding that event officials conducted a thorough review of the course.

“That review has identified an error in how this year's detour-related course adjustments were calculated and for that we sincerely apologize.

“The additional distance added for the Wellington Bridge detour was partially offset with adjustments made to the course's west end turnaround point. Upon review it was determined that the turnaround point did not fully offset the addition of the detour.”

Keogh said the Edmonton Marathon “owns this error.”

“We take full responsibility,” he wrote. “We appreciate the many participants who have emailed and the ones that we have followed up with to have additional conversations.”

Prior to the statement being issued, elite and amateur runners alike had raised concerns about the race distances. Four runners told CBC News on Monday they were convinced they ran too far.

Keogh told media outlets on Monday that the courses were measured correctly and confirmed on race day.

“While we pursued the highest level of professional course measurement and certification available, an error occurred,” Keogh said Tuesday.

Athletics Canada, the national governing body for the sport, told media on Monday that it too was confident with the course measurement and certification process. As of publication, Athletics Canada had yet to issue its own statement about the updated position being taken by the Edmonton Marathon regarding the issue.

“We are working directly with Athletics Canada and other relevant partners to determine how this year’s results can be recognized,” Keogh said in his statement Tuesday, acknowledging that the race was a qualifier for larger running events, including the Boston Marathon.

Calgary runner Mitch Walz spent a year training for the marathon in Edmonton, hoping a time of 2:59 would not only meet the 3:05 Boston Marathon qualifying standard for his 40-44 age group, but also give him enough of a buffer to be selected if too many runners achieved the standard.

Walz estimated he ran 42.2 kilometres — the official marathon distance in Edmonton — in 2:59, but his chip time when he crossed the finish line was 3:03 on Sunday morning.

On Tuesday, Walz told CBC News the past few days have been an emotional roller-coaster.

“Not only did I kind of achieve one of my goals and run as good of a race as I could have imagined or dreamed, it just feels as if it was all pulled out from underneath me,” he said.

Mitch Walz stands near the start line at the Edmonton Marathon. (Supplied by Mitch Walz)

Walz said he knew he had been hitting his paces during the first half of the race, but when he passed the course marker showing there were three kilometres left in the race, he felt deflated and couldn’t figure out what went wrong.

Knowing what he knows now, he said he is proud of his effort but wishes he could have pushed harder during the last few kilometres.

“We do not take this lightly," Keogh wrote. "We understand that every participant arrives at the start line having invested months of dedicated training, hard work, courage and deeply held goals.

“We also understand we hosted the nation's best athletes and their finishing times did not truly reflect their amazing performances.”

Walz said it would mean a lot for him to run in Boston and he hopes he could still earn a spot at that city’s race.

As to whether he would ever race the Edmonton Marathon again, he said the answer would have been no but he understands mistakes happen and would consider running at the event again.

“Moving ahead, we will review our certification processes with our partners and ensure this error does not happen again,” Keogh wrote.

World.title: Man says he was targeted in a racist tirade in downtown Halifax
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Halifax man says he was the victim of a racist tirade Saturday afternoon after a man intentionally struck his car with the bagpipes he was carrying and shouted racist language at him.

Shalu Shajan, an immigrant from India, told CBC News he had just parked his car on Lower Water Street in downtown Halifax near Prince Street.

He said a man carrying bagpipes walked over to his car and struck his side mirror with part of the instrument.

"I immediately got out and told him that he had hit my car," Shajan said. "Instead of leaving, he walked back and struck the trunk of my car as well."

Shajan said a verbal confrontation ensued and the man became increasingly aggressive and threatening.

According to Shajan, the man began shouting racist language at him and telling him "go back to your country."

"I then realized he has something to do with my race," Shajan said.

Eyewitness Raven Fox said he and his girlfriend were walking up Prince Street when they saw the incident unfold.

Fox confirmed that there was a loud verbal confrontation between the two men.

"He yelled out loud, 'You've got your PR yet?' So there was clearly some odd racial bias going on there," Fox said, referring to permanent resident status in Canada.

Fox said the man carrying the bagpipes appeared to deliberately strike Shajan's car.

"It was just very disheartening to hear that coming from a place that's seemingly known for being so kind-hearted and welcoming, and … to a person of colour as well," Fox said.

Shajan said the man was shouting just inches from his face and he was worried that the altercation would turn physical.

He said when he took out his phone to call 911, the man walked away toward the waterfront.

Shajan said he later took a photograph of the man and reported the incident to Halifax Regional Police and their hate crime unit.

He subsequently posted about the encounter in a public Facebook post.

A police spokesperson confirmed that a report had been made and the hate crime unit was determining if the interaction was hate-motivated.

Shajan said the hate crime unit contacted him and asked him if he believed the incident was a hate crime.

He said he told the police the man was directing racist language at him and he thought it was hate-motivated.

Shajan said police asked him if he wished to press charges.

"I said, well, yes, because you know, nobody should go through it," Shajan said.

Statistics Canada data indicates that reported hate crimes targeting South Asian Canadians have increased steadily in recent years.

In 2021 there were 167 reported incidents across the country. That number grew to 483 in 2025.

The Indo-Canadian Association of Nova Scotia told CBC News that while they could not comment on this specific incident, the group is deeply concerned by yet another racist incident targeting a member of the Indian diaspora.

"Incidents of hate have consequences that extend far beyond the immediate victim," vice-president Monica Rai Dua said in an email to CBC News.

"The impact of even a single act of hate can be felt by families, newcomers, international students, and generations of Canadians who simply want to live safely and contribute to their communities in Nova Scotia."

While he has experienced racist comments in the past, Saturday was the first time he feared for his physical safety, Shajan said.

He said he decided to post about his experience on Facebook publicly to help the police with their investigation and to ensure the person is held accountable.

"I just thought I should stand up against it … you don't want [that] happening to somebody else."

World.title: Who's behind viral online posts fuelling a crisis over migration in Europe?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the days leading up to the largest mass arrival of migrants to Europe in recent years, a short video posted to Instagram garnered 1.4 million views.

It shows a young man submerged up to his neck in water before panning to land in the distance. In the top-right corner, a map traces a sea route from Fnideq, Morocco, to Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern tip of Africa. Responding to comments later, the account holder claimed "we've arrived."

The video was one of many viral posts on Instagram, TikTok and other platforms that appear to have helped mobilize at least two waves of irregular migration from Morocco into Ceuta. The latest, attempted on August 15, led to dozens of arrests.

The accounts belong to several online communities that are part of a broader ecosystem focused on migration-related culture — music, memes and imagery. Some tap into, and appear to be trying to profit from, the desperation of mostly African and Middle Eastern youth seeking better lives abroad.

There is disagreement among governments and organizations over whether a single entity was behind what happened in Ceuta or whether migration was weaponized for geopolitical aims. What is clear is that misinformation, amplified by multiple online communities, helped drive this summer's waves toward Ceuta.

This photo shows a moment from a video which received 1.4 million views on Instagram, was posted just a few days before more than 72,000 people crossed the border from Morocco to Ceuta. (Instagram)

How the crossings took shape online

CBC's visual investigations team, with assistance from Sebastian Vandermeersch of the investigative collective Bellingcat, identified multiple social media accounts, particularly on Instagram, that were active ahead of the first wave on July 30.

The surge in posts was initially triggered by misinformation suggesting a Spanish court ruling meant the country would no longer turn away migrants arriving by sea. Many faceless accounts subsequently began promoting the idea the crossing was possible, using similar language and images. Some posts garnered millions of views.

The consequences were significant: more than 72,000 people crossed the border on July 30, overwhelming authorities in Ceuta and setting off a political crisis in Europe.

The vast majority of those who crossed at the end of July have since returned to Morocco, but at least 5,000 remain in Ceuta, many living on a beach with help from charities. Nearly 100 people died trying to make the crossing.

It is a stark illustration of how misinformation and manipulation can have "real-world impact" when amplified across online communities and directed at people desperate for answers, said Moustafa Ayad, executive director for Africa, the Middle East and Asia at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. His team has tracked the surge in social media activity over the past month.

A social media post highlights a section of the border fence between Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta that would be easiest to cross. (Instagram)

Some social media accounts funnelled followers toward WhatsApp chats where users planned crossings and shared information about how to reach Ceuta. Others offered advice directly in their feeds.

One Instagram video titled "the shortest distance," viewed more than 320,000 times, shows a reinforced fence topped with barbed wire and marks the Spanish and Moroccan sides with their respective flags. Large red and yellow arrows — the colours of the Spanish flag — point to a specific section. The message is clear: for someone trying to cross the fence, that is the best spot.

A BBC reporter exchanged direct messages with anonymous accounts that promised advice on entering Ceuta in exchange for money — about $750 in one case — paid up front.

Following the July 30 crossing, Meta and TikTok agreed to fact-check posts in an effort to prevent criminal organizations from using misinformation to exploit would-be migrants for profit.

But another wave of posts began building ahead of August 15, promoted as the next "window" for entering Spain by land and sea. CBC found some of the same accounts that had helped mobilize the July 30 crossing, along with many new accounts created in the days before August 15.

Several posts used variations of the message: "15/08/2026. Everything will become clear on this day."

Reports from Morocco indicate hundreds or more people made their way to the border on August 15.

An Instagram post with a variation on the date and 'Everything will become clear on this day' language. (Instagram)

This time, Moroccan and Spanish authorities were prepared. Thousands of police were deployed on both sides of the border. According to Morocco's state broadcaster, authorities arrested nearly 300 migrants that Saturday.

Ahead of the weekend, the government said it was monitoring "the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin" encouraging the crossing and would act against those responsible.

Several Instagram accounts involved in the July 30 crossing have since been disabled.

Why the messages found an audience

One factor that helped fuel the online surge was that growing numbers of migrants had successfully reached Ceuta even before the Spanish court ruling, according to the Mixed Migration Centre, a migration research organization headquartered in Geneva.

Researchers there found Ceuta, long a destination for migrants, had become the most popular entry point into Spain in the first quarter of this year. According to the International Organization for Migration, the Spanish government reported that more than 2,200 people entered by land by the end of May — three times as many as during the same period a year earlier.

The exact reason is unclear but could include stricter patrols on other migration routes.

Spanish military personnel gather at the border with Morocco in Ceuta, following mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into Spanish territory, in Ceuta, Spain, August 15, 2026. (Pedro Nunes/Reuters)

"It did play a role in the misinformation that was shaping up on social media, basically presenting a picture like, 'hey, you can make it,'" said Bram Frouws, director of the Mixed Migration Centre.

But Frouws cautioned against attributing the surge itself to social media.

"Social media [and misinformation] didn't shape the desire or the aspiration to migrate," he told CBC from the Netherlands. "The wish to migrate is already there."

Many of the accounts identified by CBC appeared to reflect widespread disillusionment and desperation among young people in North Africa and beyond, using aspirational images and language that valorize migration.

The response to the posts underlines the depth of that desperation.

People waddle through water to enter Spain, and in the background people who just entered Spain return back to Morocco, amid mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into Spanish territory, in Ceuta, Spain, July 31, 2026. (Jon Nazca/Reuters)

"People are hard up," said Ayad. For young people facing high unemployment — as high as 40 per cent among youth in Morocco, for example — and a lack of political agency or respect for their rights at home, the surge of migration-related messaging is "going to read like 'now is the time.'"

Because Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave in North Africa, provide the only land borders between Africa and a European country, many of the accounts appear to originate in North African countries, including Morocco and Algeria. Other reports suggest some originate in Italy and Turkey.

Some accounts use European or EU flags and mention a number of potential European destinations without explicitly saying they are selling a way to get there.

One account, posting days before the August 15 crossing, showed an image of the Eiffel Tower with the words "Leaving has become our only concern." Another post that day showed a map tracing a swimming route from Fnideq to Ceuta. Another said "and in the end, we will meet in Europe."

That account had changed its username six times, according to its account details. Although it had existed since June 2025, all of its posts were dated August 3.

A post from a social media account shows the Eiffel Tower and the words 'Leaving has become our only concern.' (Instagram)

Every post used a popular Arabic hashtag mentioning Germany, Belgium, Italy, Paris and "al-Ghorba."

The Arabic word "al-Ghorba" has layered meanings encompassing life abroad, exile and alienation from loved ones.

"Immigration isn't running away," says another Instagram account's bio. "It's the search for opportunity."

Influencer-style accounts with similar themes of departure are followed by thousands of people. More than one repeatedly features photos of people in wetsuits posing on beaches or treading water, an apparent reference to the swimming route from Fnideq to Ceuta.

CBC attempted to contact several accounts referencing the July 30 and August 15 waves but received no response.

World.title: 'She's our hero': Dog honoured after protecting Ontario family from black bear last fall
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A dog from Nipigon, Ont., is being recognized for her efforts to protect her family from a black bear last fall.

Chloe, a mixed-breed, medium-sized dog, has been inducted into the Purina Animal Hall of Fame, which recognizes pets " for their remarkable bravery and unwavering devotion in protecting their owners during life-threatening emergencies," a media release states.

"She's a rescue dog," said Colette Shwetz, who owns Chloe along with her husband, Joe. "We rescued her in May 2019. She was about six months old when she came to us."

"She doesn't like a lot of attention. She's just one of those old soul dogs," Colette Shwetz said, adding "she's just full of love."

That was certainly on full display the night of Sept. 16, 2025. Chloe was let out into the yard, and when she came back in, the bear followed.

"Here we are in my kitchen, the three of us, me, the dog and the bear," Colette Shwetz said.

Joe Shwetz was already asleep, but was woken up by Chloe's barking.

"I got up, run out, went into the kitchen," Joe Shwetz said. "Chloe had a hind leg, which was the bear, in her mouth, trying to pull it towards the door."

All three managed to get the bear out of the kitchen and into an adjoining hallway, and it then made its way into the basement.

Held off the bear until police arrived

Chloe "stood guard," Colette Shwetz said, barking and holding the bear off until the police arrived and dispatched it.

"We all ended up with a lot of staples and stitches and a lot of wound care," Colette Shwetz said. "Chloe, we almost lost her through the bite that she got, but she did really well. We got her through it."

And Chloe also got a steak dinner as a reward, Colette Shwetz said.

"She's our hero," she said. "I know that without her, I would not be here. That is a 100 per cent certainty."

In a media release, Purina said the hall of fame was established in 1968, and has so far recognized 198 animals — 170 dogs, 27 cats, and one horse — "for extraordinary acts of courage and devotion that have helped save lives across Canada."

Chloe isn't the only dog from northwestern Ontario in the hall of fame.

Murph, an Australian Blue Merle Sheepdog from Kenora, was inducted in 1984 after she alerted her owners to a fire in the apartment building they were living in.

Her owners then rushed to notify all the other residents, and all escaped the fire.

World.title: ‘Illegitimate’ for courts to declare a right to bike lanes
World.content:
Article content

A legal battle over Toronto’s bike lanes has turned into a bigger conversation about public policy and the role of the courts. In this interview, National Post contributor Ben Woodfinden joins Rob Breakenridge to discuss last week’s Ontario Court of Appeal decision that rejected the notion of a Charter right to bike lanes and overturned a lower court decision that blocked the Ontario government from removing a number of downtown Toronto bike lanes. Woodfinden argues that the decision is a victory for common sense and judicial restraint, helping to remind us all that policy decisions belong to elected officials, not judges. He also discusses what this means for the Charter section at the centre of this case: Section 7, which Woodfinden argues has seen a dramatically expanded interpretation since it was drafted over four decades ago. World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.
